name: Linked-List Manipulation Code Tracing
recognitionClueHinglish: C function/pointer-reassignment statements diye hain jo ek linked list ko modify karte hain, aur poocha hai resulting list kya banegi — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (24 me se 8 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Draw actual node boxes with data values and arrows — NEVER trace pointer reassignment purely in your head.
Update arrows ONE statement at a time, in the exact given order — order of reassignment matters critically (reassigning next before saving the old value loses information).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Draw the initial list as boxes connected by arrows.
2. For each statement in order, identify exactly which arrow is being redirected, and redraw it.
3. Watch for temp/auxiliary pointers used to 'save' a node before its original arrow is overwritten — a common technique in reversal/rearrangement code.
4. Read off the final list by following arrows from the head after all statements execute.
variationsObserved: Moving the last element to the front.
Recursive list-size/property computation with a fill-in-the-blank base case.
commonTraps: Overwriting a 'next' pointer before saving the node it used to point to — loses the rest of the list irrecoverably in the trace.
edgeCases: Empty list or single-node list as the starting input — trace these separately, they often break naive-looking code.

name: Insertion/Deletion Complexity Analysis (pointer-given vs search-needed)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai insert/delete ki worst-case complexity kya hai, given a pointer to some node (or given just a value to search for) — ye complexity-classification pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Separate the 'find the position' cost (O(n), unless pointer already given) from the 'modify pointers' cost (always O(1)).
Singly-list delete-given-only-the-node's-own-pointer: O(1) via the copy-next-and-delete-next trick, EXCEPT for the last node.
Doubly-list delete-given-the-node's-own-pointer: true O(1) always (has its own prev pointer).
conceptsRequired: O(1) vs O(n) distinction for find vs modify
Singly vs doubly linked list delete trade-off
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify EXACTLY what's given: a pointer to the target node? To its predecessor? Just a value to search for?
2. If a value must be searched for first: that's O(n), regardless of how fast the actual insert/delete step is.
3. If a pointer to the node itself is given in a SINGLY list: check if it could be the last node (breaks the O(1) trick) — worst case is then O(n).
variationsObserved: Maintaining SORTED order during insertion — search-for-position cost dominates.
Comparing singly vs doubly-linked delete cost head-to-head in the same question.
commonTraps: Claiming O(1) deletion in a singly linked list without checking whether the given node could be the LAST node.
edgeCases: Deleting the last node in a singly linked list with only that node's pointer given — genuinely needs O(n) (must find the predecessor).

name: Linked List vs Array (or other DS) Comparative Trade-offs
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai kaunsi operation linked list pe SLOWEST/inefficient hogi, ya linked list kis problem ke liye SUITABLE/unsuitable hai (jaise binary search, radix sort, polynomial manipulation) — ye comparative-tradeoff pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Linked list's core weakness: NO random access → binary search doesn't get its usual speedup.
Linked list's core strength: O(1) insert/delete ONCE you have the position (unlike arrays, which need O(n) shifting).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For 'which operation is slowest', check if it needs random access (binary search, direct indexing) — that's the weak point.
2. For 'is linked list suitable for X', check if X needs frequent insert/delete (suitable) vs frequent random access (not suitable).
variationsObserved: Set-operations (union, intersection, etc.) implemented via unordered linked lists — reason about which needs full traversal vs can shortcut.
Concatenation-in-O(1) requiring a specific list variant (circular doubly linked, or tail pointer maintained).
commonTraps: Assuming linked lists are 'generally worse' or 'generally better' than arrays — it's always operation-specific, never a blanket statement.

name: Circular Linked List Design (which single pointer to maintain)
recognitionClueHinglish: Circular linked list use ho raha hai (jaise Queue represent karne ke liye) aur poocha hai ek SINGLE external pointer kis node ko point kare taaki dono operations O(1) rahein.
whatShouldComeToMind: For a circular-list-as-queue: point the single external pointer to the REAR node — then front = rear->next (O(1) access to front too!), and both enqueue (insert after rear, update rear) and dequeue (remove rear->next) are O(1).
Pointing to the FRONT instead would make enqueue (reaching the rear) an O(n) traversal.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify which node needs to be reached QUICKLY for each operation.
2. Realize that pointing to REAR gives O(1) access to BOTH rear (directly) and front (via rear->next, since it's circular).
commonTraps: Assuming pointing to FRONT is equally good — it's not, since reaching REAR from FRONT needs full traversal.

name: Recursive Property-Check Function on a Linked List
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek recursive function di hai jo linked list pe koi property check karti hai (jaise sorted hai ya nahi) — poocha hai function kis condition me TRUE return karega.
whatShouldComeToMind: Trace the recursion the same way as the Recursion topic's value-tracing pattern — base cases first (empty list, single node), then combine.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the base case(s) (usually NULL list or single-node list).
2. Trace how the recursive case combines the current node's check with the recursive call's result (AND-combining for 'all satisfy' properties).
commonTraps: Missing that short-circuit AND (&&) in C means the recursive call only happens if earlier conditions already passed.
